title: L versus P
formal: Is \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\)? Equivalently, does the Circuit Value Problem have a deterministic algorithm that always halts and uses \(O(\log (n+2))\) bits of working memory on an input of binary encoding length n?
definitions: L consists of total decision languages recognized by a fixed deterministic Turing machine with a read-only input tape and a fixed finite number of initially blank read/write work tapes over fixed finite alphabets. The input can be revisited freely; all visited work-tape cells count toward space, but the read-only input itself does not. For each language there must be a constant C such that every n-bit input uses at most \(C \log _{2}(n+2)\) work bits and the machine halts. Acceptance is a final state, not a long output tape usable as memory. A halting machine in this model has only polynomially many possible configurations on a fixed input, so its time is automatically polynomial. P is the class of languages decided by uniform deterministic Turing machines in \(O((n+2)^{c})\) time for some fixed c. Circuit Value receives an explicit topologically ordered DAG of AND, OR, and NOT gates, Boolean input values, and one designated output gate, and asks whether its value is 1. The entire gate and input encoding counts toward n; malformed encodings are rejected. There are no random bits, oracle, advice, auxiliary catalytic tape, or restrictions on circuit depth. In this statement, “explicitly given/encoded/listed” means the entire finite list, table or syntax tree described above is part of the input or output, with its full encoding counted; it does not mean a circuit, oracle or program generating a larger object.
answer_criterion: Prove \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\) or \(\mathrm{L}\ne \mathrm{P}\) in the read-only-input model defined here. Equality means that every polynomial-time decision language admits a halting deterministic logarithmic-space machine; inequality means that at least one such language admits none.
why: This is a fundamental question about how much memory efficient computation needs. It asks whether all of polynomial-time reasoning can be reorganized around logarithmic working storage, and connects circuit evaluation, graph reachability, recomputation, and the structure of space-bounded complexity.

importance.reason: A canonical unresolved boundary between time and memory, asking whether any polynomial-time decision problem intrinsically needs more than logarithmic workspace.

progress.text: Ladner’s logspace completeness theorem for Circuit Value supplies a universal P-complete problem for the question.
Reingold proves undirected connectivity is in L. This resolves a major special case of low-memory graph computation without handling all directed reachability or P-complete problems.
Williams obtains the \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) deterministic space simulation and square-root-type circuit-evaluation space bounds. These remain far above logarithmic space in the general case.
Blais’s logarithmic-space notes explicitly state that strictness between these basic classes remains unknown and fix the read-only-input convention needed to formulate the question.

status_note: The Winter 2026 logarithmic-space notes explicitly leave the basic containments unresolved. A primary-source and later-result search on 11 September 2026 found no resolution of L versus P. The square-root-space simulation remains above logarithmic space for general polynomial-time computations.

context_blocks.text: A polynomial-time algorithm may keep a large table of intermediate results. A logarithmic-space algorithm has room for a fixed number of indices into its input: one position among n symbols needs about \(\log _{2} n\) bits. It can revisit the read-only input and recompute intermediate values, but it cannot retain an arbitrary n-bit table. The question asks whether this severe memory restriction still permits every polynomial-time decision task.

Circuit Value is a concrete complete problem for P under logarithmic-space reductions. Evaluating gates in topological order uses polynomial time and readily stores their values. An alternative may recompute gate values, but shared dependencies make naive recursive expansion expensive in both stack space and repeated work. Completeness says that a logarithmic-space solution to this one task would extend to all polynomial-time decision problems.

Logarithmic workspace already forces polynomial time for a halting deterministic machine: revisiting the same full configuration would produce an infinite loop. Consequently the question does not grant unlimited superpolynomial recomputation while retaining membership in L. The polynomial time exponent can nevertheless depend on the machine, so lower bounds for one fixed time budget are insufficient.

\(\mathrm{L}\subseteq \mathrm{NL}\subseteq \mathrm{P}\), where NL allows nondeterministic logarithmic-space computation. A proof that \(\mathrm{L}\ne \mathrm{NL}\) would therefore separate L from P, but \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{NL}\) would not itself settle \(\mathrm{L}=\mathrm{P}\). Reingold resolves undirected reachability in logarithmic space; directed reachability remains a separate NL-complete target, and Circuit Value represents the potentially larger class P.

Recent time-to-space simulation substantially improves general upper bounds without reaching logarithmic space. Williams simulates time t in \(O(\sqrt{t \log  t})\) space and obtains an analogous square-root-type space bound for Boolean circuit evaluation. With polynomial t, the guarantee is still polynomial space. This advances the tradeoff while leaving the much smaller \(O(\log  n)\) target unresolved.

sentences: Logarithmic-space computation can retain only a few input indices and counters while repeatedly rereading the input.
The question asks whether that memory always suffices for every polynomial-time decision problem.
Evaluating a supplied Boolean circuit is a representative complete task.
Shared dependencies make naive recomputation expensive, while storing all intermediate gate values exceeds the space budget.
The project tests whether efficient computation fundamentally needs substantial working memory or can always reorganize its information into an extremely small state.
